title: The scariest part of Silent Hill: Townfall? It's not the monsters—it's British interior design
summary: The latest Silent Hill game goes overboard with tiny details of Scottish coastal life.
body: Silent Hill: Townfall has a different kind of resonance if you grew up in the UK. Its Scottish island of St Amelia is already my favourite video game environment of the year for how it evokes the atmosphere and time of a place—specifically 1996—and captures the specific details of small town life. From the video rental shop to the bunting sadly hanging from the buildings, it's the kind of run-down fishing town you never normally see in a video game. That's probably because it's not as glamorous as somewhere like Kamurocho in Tokyo (St Amelia regrettably lacks a Sega World) or New York, and not as dreamy as the Stephen King-inflected small town settings of games like Alan Wake or Silent Hill 2. Using the Silent Hill franchise as this trojan horse to smuggle in a location that's clearly of interest to the Glasgow-based development team at Screen Burn was a marvellous idea: given the state of the games industry, it's unlikely that anyone will ever again be given the budget or time to craft an authentic British newsagent or storefront for a fish and chip shop. Still, as eerily authentic as St Amelia's exterior details are, like the telephone boxes and road signs, it's the interiors th…

title: Razer Soma Chroma gaming chair review
summary: Lights, camera, inaction! Illuminate your sitting with Razer's RGB chair.
body: Picture the scene. It’s Christmas morning, the sky is still dark, and Santa is heaving his gigantic ass through your central heating ducts. He emerges into the living room; perhaps he oozes like toothpaste, or pops out fully formed like a jelly from a mould. We’ll never know. He looks around, picks a bit of fluff out of his ear, and sees what he’s looking for: there, in the corner of the room it sits, lit up like... well, a Christmas tree. Only it’s not a spruce or fir, but a chair. Razer has reinvented the Christmas tree as something you can sit on, and its name is the Soma Chroma. Yes, literature fans, it’s got the same name as the drug used by the totalitarian state in Aldus Huxley’s Brave New World that keeps citizens perpetually happy, docile, and compliant. Perhaps it is therefore a metaphor for videogames, which famously leave their participants meek and submissive. Or maybe not. The RGB strips are only at the very top, at the sides of your head if you’re tall enough, but something about their shape distinctly recalls the angles of a Nordmann (or one of those car air fresheners that dangle from the rear-view mirror), as do the harder edges you’ll find elsewhere in contrast …

title: Sorry early adopters, Logitech is releasing an improved Superstrike making the original all but obsolete just months after launch
summary: While the new one is a great mouse, it's what the first should have been.
body: It's fair to say I was pretty taken by the G Pro X2 Superstrike when Logitech launched it earlier this year. It was the first mouse I'd seen in a long time that did something genuinely revolutionary. But, just seven months later, it is being rendered all but obsolete by the new G Pro X3 Superstrike. The revolutionary part of the original was that it made its switches analogue and paired this with haptic feedback to replicate the feeling of a click. This allows for adjustable actuation, meaning you can set it low for less time between deciding to click and actually clicking, and the haptics make sure you feel the click exactly when you should, whenever it's set to actuate. That being said, it's far from a perfect mouse. I was thoroughly enamoured by it during my testing, and I still think it deserves a heck of a lot of credit for that revolutionary tech alone. But over time its flaws have come to feel more pronounced to me. It's pretty much the same as the Superlight 2 in other respects, from the shape to the weight, side buttons, and scroll wheel. title: 'We hacked the FBI' says previous Rockstar-breaching hacking group: 'We hold data on all FBI employees and applicants'
summary: The status of the Gibson is currently unknown.
body: High-profile hacking group ShinyHunters (the very same group that demanded a ransom from GTA 6 developer Rockstar Games earlier this year) has now claimed it's managed to breach the internal databases of the US Federal Bureau of Investigations. Speaking to 404 Media , a representative of the group said that it now holds data on "all" FBI employees and applicants, while a sample provided to the outlet appears to contain the personal data of 5,000 FBI employees. According to 404, the data includes addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and "in some cases details on their spouse." Reuters was also shown a data sample by the group, and says it was able to partially verify the leaked info by running the details against existing social security numbers, credit bureau records, and previously breached data—including info on current FBI director Kash Patel. The FBI jobs website was also defaced as part of the hack, showing a message that said "this site has been seized by ShinyHunters," mimicking the message commonly seen on seized cybercriminal pages after an FBI raid. title: Halo Studios cinematic director promoted, then laid off in the same week
summary: Just when I think I can't be surprised anymore, something like this happens.
body: Not that things are great for anybody at the moment, but I'm not entirely sure how anyone in the videogame industry keeps their head together—Josh Daniels, one of the latest victims in Xbox's brutal series of resets , has been promoted and then laid off in the same week. For some context, this forms part of the previously-announced 1,600 layoffs that'll be happening as Xbox's fiscal year whirls around . This is, of course, after a 1,600-person bloodbath that preceded it, leaving a sword dangling precariously over Microsoft's remaining videogame studios. Daniels' absurd circumstances remind me of a report, which surfaced in July , that described a situation in which an anonymous source told Game Developer their layoffs "left colleagues scrambling to make sense of the situation using unofficial channels—many of which are overseen by union members and organizers." Also in July, Bethesda developers were also reportedly told they had jobs until September right before the axe swung . What's clear is this: Nothing, absolutely nothing, signals safety in the videogame industry anymore. Even if you're promoted, you can get punted from a studio in the same week .

title: Where can Australians buy R18+ PC games without a credit card? Pretty much everywhere but Steam
summary: Valve has dropped the ball on implementing reasonable age verification measures, so it's time to look further afield.
body: Valve implemented age verification for Australian Steam users earlier this month, which was inevitable: Australian law demands it . Unfortunately, Valve has opted for the most brute force, user-negligent approach possible. To buy R18+ games on Steam in Australia—to even access their store pages—you need to provide a credit card. The problem being that most Australians don't use credit cards. This study of consumer payment behaviour by the Reserve Bank of Australia bears this out: the share of payments made in Australia with credit or card charges in 2025 was 23% (versus debit cards at 49%). This is in stark contrast with the US where, according to Bankrate , 74% of adults own a credit card (and nearly half of those are in debt!). I'm not sure if Valve did its research: perhaps it did and it doesn't care. Rather than create the infrastructure to cope with age verification on Steam, or pay a contractor to do it, it's probably easier for Valve to let Australian customers be angry about it. title: Vindicated: after speaking to some pro Counter-Strike players I'm sure I was right when I said 360 Hz is the sweet spot for competitive FPS
summary: The two CS2 players I spoke to seem to agree.
body: A few months ago I made the case that a 360 Hz refresh rate on your monitor is the sweet spot for competitive FPS before diminishing returns kick in. I had nothing but my own testing and a big bottle of 'trust me bro' back then, but I've now spoken to a couple of Counter-Strike 2 pros and I remain convinced I was right. At Logitech's G Play event (featuring a Counter-Strike 2 tournament) in Warsaw earlier today, I spoke to Oscar Bell, AKA 'Azuwu', and Simon Boije, AKA 'yxngstxr'. Both currently play for Luminosity , a team that particularly tugs at my CS2 heart strings given it was very big circa 2016 when I was still lapping up the tailwinds of CS:GO novelty. Regarding refresh rates, Azuwu tells me: "When I had 240 at home, I didn't even really notice 360. But now I'm 360 I can't go back down, you know, I feel it a lot. So I think 360, 400, 600 are all pretty similar... I'd say 400 is a nice spot and 600 is extra nice. But anyway, in a lot of PCs, you won't hit 600 frames." And Yxngstxr says: "I think it's kind of a placebo, personal thing, you know? Because on most PCs you rarely get 600 fps, right?... 600 Hz with like 300 fps, it doesn't even matter." Hired in 2000, Le ultimately spent six years with the company, witnessing impactful moments of Valve history—moments like Gabe Newell's Mongolian throat singing phase. title: I set out to prove polling rate affects my aim and instead found my favourite DPI setting
summary: The polling rate boot camp was worth it, but for a different reason.
body: I'm a thoroughly average gamer. And in first-person shooters, I reckon I am ever so slightly above average at aiming—If aim-tester software, Aimlabs, is anything to go by, at least (top 38%, baby). But as a hardware tester, I have access to all kinds of gaming gear, and that includes competitive-level specs. I wanted to see if the average gamer would benefit from a better polling rate and, as the average gamer, I thought I was the perfect guinea pig. So, grabbing my Asus Rog Harpe II Extreme Edition 20 , a mouse with a max DPI of 65,000 and a max polling rate of 8,000 Hz, I went through the training software at different polling rates multiple times to see if it would improve my aim. If you are unaware of what exactly a polling rate is, it is the rate at which your gaming mouse communicates with your rig. A 125 Hz polling rate gives feedback to your PC every 8 milliseconds, whereas 8,000 Hz gives feedback every 0.125 milliseconds. Generally speaking, the advice for most gamers is to linger at around 1,000 Hz, as responding every millisecond is plenty fast but not so fast that it drains the battery life of your squeaker.
